title: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context

topics.title: Planning: meaning, sectoral and regional planning

learn.hook: From 1951 to 2017, India ran its economy through Five Year Plans. Why plan at all — and plan for whom: sectors or regions?
points: Planning is the process of thinking, formulating a scheme or programme and implementing a set of actions to achieve some goal.
In India, planning was done through Five Year Plans prepared by the Planning Commission, set up in 1950; the First Five Year Plan began in 1951.

Sectoral planning: formulating and implementing schemes for development of various sectors of the economy — agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services.
Regional planning: development is not uniform over space; some regions are more developed than others, so regional planning aims to reduce regional imbalances in development.

example.q: A state draws up a plan to build roads, schools and irrigation specifically for its backward southern districts. Is this sectoral or regional planning?
steps: The plan targets a particular region (backward districts).
Its aim is to reduce imbalance with other regions.
So it is regional planning.

learn.reallife: The Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) focuses on 112 lagging districts — a modern example of regional planning.

topics.title: NITI Aayog and target area planning

learn.hook: On 1 January 2015, the 65-year-old Planning Commission was replaced by a 'think tank' — NITI Aayog.
points: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. It acts as a think tank giving strategic and technical advice to the Central and State Governments, follows a bottom-up, decentralised approach and promotes cooperative federalism.
To arrest growing regional and social disparities, the Planning Commission introduced target area and target group approaches.
Target area programmes: Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Programme, Desert Development Programme and Hill Area Development Programme.
Target group programmes: Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA) and Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA).
In the Eighth Five Year Plan, special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas.

example.q: Classify: Drought Prone Area Programme, Small Farmers Development Agency, Hill Area Development Programme, Marginal Farmers Development Agency.
steps: Programmes for a type of area → target area: DPAP, HADP.
Programmes for a group of people → target group: SFDA, MFDA.
example.answer: Target area: DPAP, HADP; target group: SFDA, MFDA

learn.reallife: NITI Aayog ranks states on the SDG India Index and health and education indicators — encouraging competitive and cooperative federalism.

learn.hook: Apple orchards in Uttarakhand, tea in Darjeeling, Nilgiri dairy cooperatives — hill development must suit the hills.
points: The Hill Area Development Programme was initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan, covering 15 districts: all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (now Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu.

The National Committee on the Development of Backward Areas (1981) recommended that all hill areas with a height above 600 m and not covered under the tribal sub-plan be treated as backward hill areas.
Detailed plans were drawn to harness indigenous resources through horticulture, plantation agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry, and small-scale and village industries.
The plans were to take into account the topography, ecological, social and economic conditions of each area.

example.q: Why would large heavy industries not be a suitable focus for hill area development?
steps: Hill topography is rugged and the ecology fragile.
Plans must suit local topography, ecology and resources.
So horticulture, plantations, animal husbandry, forestry and small industries are better.
example.answer: They don't suit hill topography and fragile ecology; local-resource activities do

learn.reallife: Himachal's apple economy and Uttarakhand's organic farming and homestays reflect the HADP idea of using local resources.

topics.title: Drought Prone Area Programme: aims and approach

learn.hook: In a drought year, a farmer in Marathwada loses his crop and his income. DPAP tried to give him work — and long-term water security.
points: The Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets.
Initially it emphasised the construction of labour-intensive civil works.

Later it emphasised irrigation projects, land development programmes, afforestation, grassland development and creation of basic rural infrastructure such as electricity, roads, markets, credit and services.
The National Committee on Development of Backward Areas found that the programme was largely confined to agriculture and allied sectors, with a major focus on restoration of ecological balance.

example.q: Why did DPAP shift from labour-intensive civil works to irrigation, afforestation and grassland development?
steps: Civil works gave short-term jobs but not lasting drought-proofing.
Irrigation, afforestation and pastures build productive assets and restore ecology.
These reduce the impact of future droughts.
example.answer: To create lasting productive assets and restore ecological balance

learn.reallife: MGNREGA works like farm ponds, check dams and tree planting continue the DPAP idea of employment plus drought-proofing assets.

topics.title: Drought-prone areas of India and watershed approach

learn.hook: Rajasthan, Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Telangana — these names often appear in drought headlines. Why these regions?
points: Growing population pressure forces people to use marginal lands for agriculture, causing ecological degradation; so alternative employment opportunities are needed in drought-prone areas.
The strategy for these areas is an integrated watershed development approach at the micro level: restoring ecological balance among water, soil, plants, and human and animal populations.

In 1967 the Planning Commission identified 67 districts (entirely or partly) as drought-prone; in 1972 the Irrigation Commission introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area to demarcate drought-prone areas.

Drought-prone areas mostly cover the semi-arid and arid tracts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Marathwada (Maharashtra), the Rayalaseema and Telangana plateaus, the Karnataka plateau and the highlands and interior parts of Tamil Nadu.
Drought-prone areas of Punjab, Haryana and northern Rajasthan are largely protected because of the spread of irrigation.

example.q: A district has 18% of its net sown area irrigated and gets low, erratic rainfall. Is it drought-prone by the Irrigation Commission's criterion?
steps: The 1972 criterion uses 30% irrigated area.
With low, erratic rainfall, it would be classed as drought-prone.
example.answer: Yes — its irrigated area is below the 30% criterion

learn.reallife: Maharashtra's Jalyukt Shivar Abhiyan built check dams and farm ponds in Marathwada villages using a watershed approach.

learn.hook: High in the Himachal Himalayas, the Gaddi shepherds of Bharmaur move their flocks with the seasons, speaking their own Gaddiali dialect.
points: The Bharmaur tribal area comprises the Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh; it has been a notified tribal area since 21 November 1975.
It is inhabited by the Gaddis, a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region; they practised transhumance and converse in the Gaddiali dialect.

The region has harsh climatic conditions, a low resource base and a fragile environment. The Ravi and its tributaries, the Budhil and Tundahen, drain it and carve deep gorges; it lies between the Dhaula Dhar range (south) and Pir Panjal (north) and has four physiographic divisions — Holi, Khani, Kugti and Tundah.
Winters are freezing with snowfall (mean January temperature about 4°C); summers are mild (July about 26°C). Gaddis traditionally migrate to lower areas in winter.

The economy was based on agriculture and allied activities like sheep and goat rearing; the region was economically and socially backward and isolated. On a map, Bharmaur lies in Chamba district in the north-west of Himachal Pradesh.

example.q: What is the difference between the mean July and January temperatures in Bharmaur?
steps: July ≈ 26°C; January ≈ 4°C.
Difference = 26 − 4 = 22°C.

learn.reallife: Gaddi shepherds still move flocks between Chamba's high pastures and Kangra's lower valleys — a living tradition of transhumance.

topics.title: Bharmaur: Integrated Tribal Development Project and outcomes

learn.hook: In 1971, fewer than 2 in 100 women in Bharmaur could read. By 2011, about 65 did. What changed?
points: Development of Bharmaur began in the 1970s when the Gaddis were included among Scheduled Tribes. The tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 under the Fifth Five Year Plan, and Bharmaur was designated as one of five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh.

Aim: improve the quality of life of the Gaddis and narrow the gap in development between Bharmaur and other areas of Himachal Pradesh; highest priority to transport and communications, agriculture and allied activities, and social and community services.

Outcomes: infrastructure — schools, health care facilities, potable water, roads, communications and electricity. Villages along the Ravi in Holi and Khani areas benefited most; remote villages in Tundah and Kugti are still outside the ambit of development.

Social benefits: big rise in literacy, improved sex ratio and decline in child marriage; female literacy rose from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011, and the gender gap in literacy declined.

Economic change: shift from subsistence agro-pastoral economy (foodgrains, livestock) to more pulses and cash crops (though with traditional tools); only about one-tenth of households now practise transhumance, and many Gaddis migrate to Kangra and nearby areas in winter for wage labour.

example.q: By how many percentage points did female literacy in Bharmaur rise from 1971 to 2011?
steps: Increase = 65 − 1.88 = 63.12 percentage points.

learn.reallife: Roads and schools under ITDP connected Holi and Khani villages to Chamba town, opening jobs and colleges to young Gaddis.

learn.hook: In 1987, a commission led by Norway's Prime Minister gave the world a definition of development that every exam still asks for.
points: The concept of development has changed: earlier it meant economic growth (GNP, per capita income); later it came to include social welfare and qualitative change in people's lives.
In the late 1960s, growing environmental awareness in the western world was reflected in books like 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich (1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows and others (1972).

The United Nations set up the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), headed by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland; its report 'Our Common Future' (1987), also called the Brundtland Report, popularised sustainable development.
Sustainable development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It integrates ecological, social and economic aspects of development; the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (adopted in 2015) carry this idea forward.

example.q: A town wants to grow by cutting down its watershed forest for housing. Using the Brundtland definition, explain why this may not be sustainable.
steps: It meets present housing needs.
But it destroys the forest that protects water and soil for the future.
This compromises future generations' ability to meet their needs.
example.answer: It meets present needs at the cost of future generations

topics.title: Indira Gandhi Canal: origin, stages and command area

learn.hook: A canal running hundreds of kilometres through the Thar desert, parallel to the Pakistan border — the Indira Gandhi Canal turned sand into fields.
points: The Indira Gandhi Canal (earlier the Rajasthan Canal) is one of the largest canal systems in India; conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, it was launched on 31 March 1958.
It originates at the Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to the Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in the Thar desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.
The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km, serving a culturable command area of 19.63 lakh hectares; about 70 per cent was to be irrigated by flow and the rest by lift irrigation.

Stage I: command area in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern Bikaner districts; gently undulating topography; culturable command area 5.53 lakh ha; irrigation from the early 1960s. Stage II: Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts; desert with shifting sand dunes and summer temperatures up to 50°C; command area 14.10 lakh ha; irrigation from the mid-1980s.
In lift canals, water is lifted up to make it flow against the slope of the land. Map reading: trace the canal from Harike (Punjab) south-west through Ganganagar to Jaisalmer and Barmer.

example.q: Check that the two stages add up to the total culturable command area.
steps: Stage I = 5.53 lakh ha; Stage II = 14.10 lakh ha.
This equals the total command area.

learn.reallife: Ganganagar, once desert, is now called the 'food basket of Rajasthan' thanks to Stage I of the canal.

topics.title: Indira Gandhi Canal: positive and negative impacts

learn.hook: Where camels once grazed on bajra stubble, farmers now grow wheat and cotton — but some fields have turned white with salt.
points: Positive impacts: availability of soil moisture increased; afforestation and pasture development programmes greened the land; soil erosion, wind erosion and siltation of canals reduced; canal water also met drinking water needs.
Agricultural changes: cultivated area and intensity of cropping increased tremendously.
Traditional crops — gram, bajra and guar — have been replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice.
Negative impacts: intensive irrigation and excessive use of water have led to the twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity, raising doubts about long-term sustainability.

example.q: Why does excessive canal irrigation in a desert cause soil salinity?
steps: Too much water raises the water table (waterlogging).
In high heat, water evaporates from the surface.
Dissolved salts are left behind on the soil — salinity.
example.answer: Waterlogging plus high evaporation leaves salts on the surface

learn.reallife: Parts of the canal command area now need drainage and gypsum treatment to reclaim salt-affected soils.

topics.title: Sustainable development in the canal area: water and land measures

learn.hook: Warabandi: a rotating timetable that gives every farmer on a canal outlet a fair turn of water. Simple idea, big impact!
points: The first and foremost requirement is strict implementation of the water management policy: protective irrigation in Stage I, and extensive irrigation of crops and pasture development in Stage II.
The cropping pattern should not include water-intensive crops; people should be encouraged to grow plantation crops such as citrus fruits instead.

Command Area Development (CAD) programmes — lining of watercourses, land development and levelling, and the warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of an outlet) — should be implemented to reduce conveyance loss of water.
Areas affected by waterlogging and soil salinity should be reclaimed.

example.q: Why is lining of watercourses an important CAD measure?
steps: Unlined channels lose water by seepage into sandy soil.
Seepage raises the water table and causes waterlogging.
Lining reduces conveyance loss and waterlogging.
example.answer: It cuts seepage losses and reduces waterlogging

learn.reallife: Kinnow and other citrus orchards around Ganganagar show how less water-intensive plantation crops can thrive with canal water.

topics.title: Sustainable development in the canal area: ecology, people and economy

learn.hook: Rows of trees planted as shelterbelts now break the desert winds that once buried canals in sand.
points: Eco-development through afforestation, shelterbelt plantation and pasture development is necessary, particularly in the fragile environment of Stage II.
Social sustainability requires that land allottees with poor economic backgrounds be given adequate financial and institutional support to cultivate their land.

Agriculture and allied activities must develop along with other sectors of the economy (like agro-processing and marketing), diversifying the economic base and linking villages, agro-service centres and market centres.

Exam focus: DPAP, ITDP and IGC case studies; sectoral vs regional planning; target area planning; HADP; Bharmaur outcomes; the concept of sustainable development; and measures for sustainability in the canal command area.

example.q: Why are shelterbelts especially important in Stage II of the canal area?
steps: Stage II has shifting sand dunes and strong winds.
Shelterbelts (rows of trees) break wind speed.
They reduce wind erosion and protect canals and fields from sand.
example.answer: They break desert winds and reduce erosion and sand deposition

learn.reallife: Food parks and mandis in Ganganagar and Hanumangarh help farmers process and sell kinnow, cotton and wheat — diversifying the canal economy.
